slots.text:
Screen Capture Rectification and
Temporal Stabilization for
Real-world Captured-screen Videos

Rongshuo Wen  124020369      Bihua Wen  124090670
Mingrui Liu  124090375

Motivation.  Screen demoiréing and screen-image restoration show captured-screen content is a real image-processing problem — yet most datasets start after the screen is already cropped, aligned, or paired with a clean reference.
Real phone-captured video is far less controlled: background clutter, perspective, glare, moiré, and dynamic on-screen content. We tackle this missing geometric preprocessing step.
Our stage:  handheld capture  →  rectified screen
Downstream enabled:  video demoiréing on the stable output
This project is the geometry stage BEFORE restoration: locate, rectify, and stabilize the screen.

slides.text_summary:
THE GAP WE FILL
Problem & Goal
The gap
▸  Resent researchs assumes the screen is already cropped & aligned.
▸  Real handheld video has off-screen background, perspective tilt, and frame-to-frame jitter.
▸  Weak borders, glare and moiré make a single frame-by-frame detector unstable.
Goal.  Continuously estimate the screen plane and render its content as a front-facing video that:
•  suppresses non-screen background & perspective
•  reduces hand-held jitter while keeping true content motion

▸  Resent researchs assumes the screen is already cropped & aligned.
▸  Real handheld video has off-screen background, perspective tilt, and frame-to-frame jitter.
▸  Weak borders, glare and moiré make a single frame-by-frame detector unstable.

Goal.  Continuously estimate the screen plane and render its content as a front-facing video that:
•  suppresses non-screen background & perspective
•  reduces hand-held jitter while keeping true content motion
•  preserves physical aspect ratio  (default 1920×1080)
Same frame: raw handheld input  →  rectified, stable screen output

slots.text: Method — Screen Motion vs. Content Motion
Core distinction:  estimate the homography from the physical screen border, and treat motion inside the screen as content — not camera — motion.

•  Edge filtering + LSD / Hough locate the four screen borders.
•  The main homography is anchored to this physical boundary

•  Inner Lucas–Kanade points serve as a consistency signal.
•  labelled screen-content motion and excluded from H estimation if conflicts

•  Low border confidence or an invalid quadrilateral triggers re-detection.
•  If recovery fails, freeze the last valid Hₜ and flag invalid regions.
Normalized output over time  (content moves, frame stays aligned)
Result:  in-screen content changes over time, yet each frame stays rectified and plane-aligned — screen motion removed, content motion preserved.

WHAT WE MEASURE
Evaluation Metrics
1
Geometric accuracy
•  Corner error on annotated key frames
•  Quadrilateral IoU
•  Aspect-ratio error
Is the screen located & rectified correctly?
2
Temporal stability
•  Residual adjacent-frame translation (px)
•  Residual rotation (deg) & scale change
•  Reported as p95 of the normalized video
How much jitter remains after normalization?
3
Signal preservation
•  Mean gradient magnitude on texture patches
•  Edge-preservation index (same screen scale)
•  2D

These measures tie geometric correctness, video stability and signal preservation together — with no dependence on a downstream restoration model.

slides.text_summary:
BORDER-GUIDED TRACKING WINS
Initial Results & Timeline
Same input video · residual translation p95 over the last 2 s (lower = steadier)
0.118 px  residual jitter
Reference-plane (border-guided) tracking cuts residual motion ~16× vs. per-frame detection (1.927) and optical-flow tracking (1.929).
Final report will compare three strategies:
Per-frame detection — re-detects each frame — jittery
Optical-flow tracking — drifts with on-screen content
Border-guided (ours) — stable, content-aware
